Here the inverse image carries the restricted structure sheaf, as in [[def-affine-open-subscheme]], and $f$ is a morphism of locally ringed spaces as in [[def-morphism-of-schemes]]. The empty scheme is affine, being $\operatorname{Spec}0$.

An **$S$-scheme** is a scheme $X$ equipped with a morphism $X\to S$. An **$S$-morphism** $X\to Y$ is a scheme morphism commuting with the maps to $S$. For $n\geq0$, choose an affine open cover $S=\bigcup_i\operatorname{Spec}A_i$. Over each chart take $\operatorname{Spec}A_i[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$. On overlaps, localization in the coefficients gives canonical isomorphisms that fix the variables; these satisfy the cocycle condition and glue by `thm-gluing-affine-schemes`. The result, independent of the cover up to the unique $S$-isomorphism respecting the coefficient maps and the ordered coordinate functions $t_1,\ldots,t_n$, is the relative affine space $\mathbf A^n_S$.

A proper ideal $P\subsetneq R$ is **prime** when $ab\in P$ implies $a\in P$ or $b\in P$. A proper ideal $M\subsetneq R$ is **maximal** when there is no proper ideal strictly between $M$ and $R$; equivalently, it is a maximal element of the poset of proper ideals ordered by inclusion.
An **integral domain**, or simply a **domain**, is a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]) $R$ such that - **(D1)** $1 \ne 0$ in $R$; - **(D2)** $R$ has no zero divisors.
For a Noetherian topological space $T$, define $\dim T$ as the supremum of the lengths $s$ of strict chains $Z_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq Z_s$ of nonempty irreducible closed subsets of $T$.

For an arbitrary base scheme $S$ define $$\mathbb P^n_S=S\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z}\mathbb P^n_{\mathbb Z},$$ with structure morphism the projection to $S$ ([[thm-fibre-products-of-schemes-exist]], [[def-scheme-over-base]]), and call the open subschemes $U^S_i=S\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z}U_i$ the **standard charts over $S$**; each is affine over $S$, and they form an open cover of $\mathbb P^n_S$. When $S=\operatorname{Spec}A$ is affine, each $U^S_i$ is the affine scheme $\operatorname{Spec}A[x^{(i)}_\ell:\ell\ne i]$. Because base change preserves open immersions and fibre products, the transition isomorphisms on $U^S_i\cap U^S_j$ are the base changes of the displayed ones, so the charts and their overlaps commute with base change.

We say that $\mathcal F$ is a **sheaf** if for every open set $U \subseteq X$ and every open cover $U=\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i$, including the empty cover of $\varnothing$, the following two conditions hold. **Locality.** If $s,t\in\mathcal F(U)$ satisfy $$s|_{U_i}=t|_{U_i}\qquad\text{for all }i\in I,$$ then $s=t$. **Gluing.** If sections $s_i\in\mathcal F(U_i)$ satisfy $$s_i|_{U_i\cap U_j}=s_j|_{U_i\cap U_j}\qquad\text{for all }i,j\in I,$$ then there exists $s\in\mathcal F(U)$ such that $$s|_{U_i}=s_i\qquad\text{for all }i\in I.$$ By locality, such a section $s$ is automatically unique.
The canonical map $A\to\Gamma(\operatorname{Spec}A,\mathcal O)$ is an isomorphism, including when $A=0$.
For $f\in A$, $\Gamma(D(f),\mathcal O)=A_f$. If $D(g)\subseteq D(f)$, the restriction is the canonical localization map $A_f\to A_g$.

Let $R,S$ be commutative rings, let $\varphi\colon R\to S$ be a unital ring homomorphism, and let $s\in S$. There is a unique unital ring homomorphism $$ \operatorname{ev}_{\varphi,s}\colon R[x]\to S $$ that extends $\varphi$ on constant polynomials and sends $x$ to $s$. It is given by $\operatorname{ev}_{\varphi,s}(\sum_i a_i x^i)=\sum_i\varphi(a_i)s^i$.
$R/P$ is an integral domain if and only if $P$ is a prime ideal. Here $R$ is commutative and $P\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}R$ is an ideal.
First isomorphism theorem for rings: $R/\ker f\cong\operatorname{im}f$.
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $a\in R$, and $f\in R[x]$. Then $f(a)=0$ if and only if $x-a$ divides $f$ in $R[x]$. More precisely, there is a unique $q\in R[x]$ such that $f=q(x-a)+f(a)$.
If $R$ is an integral domain, then $R[x]$ is an integral domain.
A morphism $j:U\to X$ is an **open immersion** if it identifies $U$ isomorphically with an open subscheme of $X$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement. > Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function > ([[def-choice-function]]). Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty, there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $S$ be a scheme and let $n\ge0$. Then the structure morphism $$\pi:\mathbb P^n_S\longrightarrow S$$ is proper.
For every field $K$ and every finite $d\ge0$, the ring $K[x_1,\ldots,x_d]$ is Noetherian: each ideal of it has a finite generating list. The proof uses only finite selections and is choice-free.
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring. Then $\operatorname{Spec}(R)$ is a Noetherian topological space.

The space $X$ is **Noetherian** when every ascending chain $$ U_0\subseteq U_1\subseteq U_2\subseteq\cdots $$ of open subsets stabilizes. Equivalently, $X$ is Noetherian when every descending chain $$ F_0\supseteq F_1\supseteq F_2\supseteq\cdots $$ of closed subsets stabilizes.
For every open cover $T=\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i$ of a Noetherian space, $\dim T=\sup_i\dim U_i$, with empty supremum $-\infty$.

If $T\subseteq R$, define its **vanishing set** by $$ V(T)=\{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}(R):T\subseteq\mathfrak p\}. $$ For an ideal $I\trianglelefteq R$ this is simply $$ V(I)=\{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}(R):I\subseteq\mathfrak p\}.

An **integral scheme** is a nonempty scheme that is reduced and whose underlying topological space is irreducible. Equivalently, it is nonempty and every nonempty affine open is the spectrum of a domain. The latter criterion is independent of the chosen affine open cover.
A morphism of schemes $f:X\to S$ is **proper** if and only if it is separated, of finite type, and universally closed.
The space $X$ is **irreducible** when $X\neq\varnothing$ and whenever $$ X=F_1\cup F_2 $$ with $F_1,F_2\subseteq X$ closed, one has $X=F_1$ or $X=F_2$.
$R/M$ is a field if and only if $M$ is a maximal ideal. Here $R$ is commutative and $M$ is an ideal of $R$.

For a scheme $X$, let $\mathcal N_X$ be the ideal sheaf whose germs are the nilpotent elements of the local rings of $X$; equivalently, a section lies in $\mathcal N_X(U)$ when it is locally nilpotent on $U$.
The ring $R$ is **reduced** when $\operatorname{Nil}(R)=(0)$, equivalently when the only nilpotent element of $R$ is $0$.
An affine scheme is **reduced** if (equivalently, for every) coordinate ring $A$ is reduced.
A point $x$ is a **generic point** of a closed subset $Z$ if $\overline{\{x\}}=Z$. For a prime $\mathfrak p$ of $A$, the point $\mathfrak p$ is generic for $V(\mathfrak p)$.

The **closure** of $A$ is $\overline{A} := \bigcap \{\, F \subseteq X : F \text{ closed and } A \subseteq F \,\}$. - The **exterior** of $A$ is $\operatorname{ext}(A) := \operatorname{int}(X \setminus A)$. - The **boundary** of $A$ is $\partial A := \overline{A} \setminus \operatorname{int}(A)$. - $x$ is a **limit point** (accumulation point) of $A$ if every neighbourhood $N$ of $x$ satisfies $N \cap (A \setminus \{x\}) \ne \varnothing$. The set of limit points of $A$ is the **derived set** $A'$. - $x$ is an **isolated point of $A$** if $x \in A$ and some neighbourhood $N$ of $x$ satisfies $N \cap A = \{x\}$. **Both operators are well posed, and the two names are justified rather than asserted.** The interior is a union of open sets, hence open by (T2), it is contained in $A$, and it contains every open $U \subseteq A$: so $\operatorname{int}(A)$ is *the largest open subset of $A$*. The family being intersected in the definition of $\overline{A}$ is nonempty, since $X$ is closed and contains $A$, so the intersection is a set; it is closed by (C2) of [[def-topological-space]], it contains $A$, and it is contained in every closed $F \supseteq A$: so $\overline{A}$ is *the smallest closed superset of $A$*.

derivations.claim: If the structure morphism f : X -> Spec k were affine, then since Spec k is an affine open subscheme of itself and the inverse image of an affine open under an affine morphism is affine, X = f^{-1}(Spec k) would be an affine scheme; this is the standing hypothesis to be refuted.

For a field k the standard charts of P^1_k are U_0 = Spec k[t] and U_inf = Spec k[u], open subschemes covering P^1_k, with overlap W = U_0 cap U_inf = Spec k[t,t^{-1}] identified with Spec k[u,u^{-1}] by t = u^{-1}; global sections are Gamma(U_0) = k[t], Gamma(U_inf) = k[u], and the restriction maps to the overlap are the localizations k[t] -> k[t,t^{-1}] and k[u] -> k[u,u^{-1}] composed with the identification.

The evaluation map k[t] -> k at t = 0 has kernel (t) because t maps to 0 and any polynomial with zero constant term is divisible by t; its image is k, a field, so (t) is prime by the domain criterion and maximal by the field-quotient criterion, and (0) is prime because k[t] is a domain; the two ideals differ, so via the injective chart inclusion they give two distinct points of P^1_k, and (t) is a maximal ideal of k[t].
If X is affine then the quasi-inverse property of the equivalence between commutative rings and affine schemes gives a canonical isomorphism X = Spec Gamma(X,O_X); set Gamma := Gamma(X,O_X).

The sheaf axioms applied to the open cover {U_0,U_inf} identify the global sections of the structure sheaf of P^1_k with the matching pairs (a,b) in k[t] x k[u] satisfying a(t) = b(t^{-1}) in k[t,t^{-1}] under the overlap identification u = t^{-1}.

P^1_k is nonempty, proper over k by the properness of relative projective space, hence of finite type because proper morphisms are of finite type; the chart rings k[t] and k[u] are Noetherian by the direct finite-variable polynomial Noetherian theorem, so their spectra U_0 and U_inf are Noetherian topological spaces, and a descending chain of closed subsets of P^1_k restricts to descending chains on the two charts and hence stabilizes, so P^1_k is Noetherian by the chain characterization.

The prime ideals (0) subsetneq (t) of k[t] produce a strict chain V((t)) = {(t)} subsetneq V((0)) = U_0 of nonempty closed subsets of U_0, using maximality of (t) for the singleton description of V((t)) and the fact that every prime contains (0); both are irreducible, a singleton because any closed cover has a member equal to the whole space and U_0 because (0) is generic for V((0)) = U_0 and hence dense, so a closed cover of U_0 has a member containing (0) and equal to U_0; therefore dim U_0 >= 1 and the dimension of an open cover gives dim P^1_k >= 1.

By the global-functions theorem Gamma is a finite field extension of k, hence a field whose only ideals are (0) and Gamma, and (0) is prime; since (0) is a proper ideal, Spec Gamma consists of the single point (0).

Writing b = sum_{j=0}^{e} b_j u^j and clearing denominators in the matching relation a(t) = b(t^{-1}) gives t^e a(t) = sum_{j=0}^{e} b_j t^{e-j}; degree comparison forces deg a = 0 when a is nonzero, so a is constant and b equals the same constant, and when a = 0 both entries vanish; hence Gamma(P^1_k,O) = k.

The isomorphism X = Spec Gamma is a bijection on points, so the hypothesis that X has more than one point is contradicted; therefore the structure morphism is not affine and X is not an affine scheme over k. Under the statement's AC assumption, this is exactly the repaired title claim for proper integral finite-type k-schemes with multiple points.

If P^1_k were affine over k, the affine case argument applied to its structure morphism together with Gamma(P^1_k,O) = k would give P^1_k = Spec k, which has exactly one point, contradicting the two distinct points found in the chart U_0; hence P^1_k is not affine over k.

If the underlying Noetherian space of X has positive dimension, then there are nonempty irreducible closed subsets Z_0 subsetneq Z_1, and choosing a point from each exhibits two distinct points of X without any choice beyond two nonempty sets; the affine case then makes X nonaffine, so no nonempty proper integral finite-type k-scheme of positive Noetherian dimension is affine over k.

P^1_k is nonempty; it is reduced because the nilpotent-germ ideal sheaf restricts to the nilpotent-germ sheaf of each chart, where it vanishes since k[t] and k[u] are domains, hence reduced rings and reduced affine schemes, and the two charts cover; it is irreducible because the open irreducible chart U_0 is dense (its overlap with U_inf is D(u), which contains the generic point (0) of U_inf) and a dense irreducible subspace has irreducible closure; hence P^1_k is nonempty, reduced and irreducible, so integral. AC enters only through the AC-carrying suppliers cited in steps 2.3 and 3.1 and in this step list.

boundaries.evidence: The empty case is excluded where it matters and included where the definitions require it. X is nonempty by the statement hypothesis, and the contradiction argument of step 4.1 needs that X has more than one point; the empty scheme is never claimed to be nonaffine. P^1_k is nonempty by the two explicit points of step 1.3, so the integrality conclusion of step 6.1 is not asserted for an empty space; note that the empty scheme is affine and is therefore correctly outside the claimed class. The charts U_0 and U_inf are nonempty, and their overlap D(u) is nonempty because u is a nonzero element of the domain k[u], which is what lets step 6.1 use the generic point (0) of U_inf.

The zero cases are handled explicitly: the zero ideal (0) of k[t] is prime because k[t] is a domain (step 1.3) and serves as the generic point of U_0 in step 2.4; the zero polynomial is separated from every degree statement in step 3.2 because the degree definition excludes it, and the case b = 0 is absorbed by taking e = 0; (0) is a proper ideal of the field Gamma because Gamma is a field, so the spectrum of Gamma in step 3.1 has the single point (0) and not the zero ring; and the kernel (t) is not the zero ideal, which is exactly what makes the two points distinct in step 1.3.

The unit and one-point situations appear in three places. The one-point space Spec Gamma of step 3.1 is the contradiction with the hypothesis that X has more than one point in step 4.1; the singleton {(t)} = V((t)) is the lower member of the strict irreducible chain in step 2.4, using that a one-point space admits no proper nonempty closed cover; and the unit 1 is used through the unital ring homomorphism ev in step 1.3 and the constant terms in step 3.2, with no claim about the case of a single point of P^1_k, which has two.

Degenerate configurations are all excluded by the argument rather than assumed away: k[t] is a domain by the polynomial-ring domain theorem, so (t) is a prime and even maximal ideal in step 1.3 and the quotient k[t]/(t) is a field, not the zero ring; the field extension Gamma/k of step 3.1 is a domain with 1 != 0, so its zero ideal is prime; the chain V((t)) subsetneq V((0)) of step 2.4 is strict precisely because (t) is a nonzero maximal ideal; and no chart or overlap is allowed to be empty, D(u) being nonempty since u is a nonzero polynomial over the field k.

There is no free numerical parameter, so the extreme cases are structural. The minimal case of the dimension claim is dim U_0 = 1, witnessed by the length-one chain of step 2.4; the affine case (X = Spec Gamma) and the projective case (P^1_k) are the two opposite ends of the argument and both are treated, with k allowed to be any field including the prime fields; the case n = 1 of projective space is the only one used, and the properness input explicitly includes n = 1 with no Noetherian or nonemptiness hypothesis on the base; and the exponent e = 0 in step 3.2 handles the endpoint of a constant polynomial b.

AC is assumed in the statement and is used exactly through the AC-carrying suppliers F1 (global functions on a proper integral variety), F22 (properness of relative projective space), F24 (spectrum of a Noetherian ring is a Noetherian space) and the construction F9 inside the AC-qualified definition of P^1_k; step 6.1 records this accounting. The remaining arguments make no infinite selections: step 5.1 selects one point from each of two nonempty closed sets, step 3.2 selects finitely many polynomial coefficients, and step 1.3 uses the explicit element t and the explicit evaluation map, so the axiom is not used for any of those. The polynomial Noetherian supplier F23 is explicitly choice-free.

boundaries.reason: The statement asserts no biconditional. The forward implications actually used are one-way: properness implies finite type (steps 2.3), a field quotient implies maximality of the ideal (step 1.3), maximality implies the singleton description of V((t)) (step 2.4), and nonempty plus reduced plus irreducible gives integrality (step 6.1); none is used in reverse.

No converse of any displayed criterion is asserted. In particular the argument never claims that an affine positive-dimensional scheme fails to exist, never claims a converse of the integrality characterization, and never claims that reducedness or irreducibility can be checked only on the two named charts; the open-cover arguments of steps 2.3 and 6.1 are used in the direction that produces the conclusion.

The two readings do agree, but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is [[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], and no item of this library may use the ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading makes compactness a property of the topological space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ alone. For $D(g)\subseteq D(f)$ the restriction maps of the two sheaves correspond under $\delta_g$ and $\delta_f$, since restriction in both is the canonical localisation (of $M\otimes_AN$, of $M$ and of $N$) and the tensor of the localisation maps is the localisation of the tensor [F3, F5]; hence the compatible maps $\delta_f$ on the basis of distinguished opens determine a morphism of $\mathcal O_U$-modules $$\delta:\widetilde{(M\otimes_AN)}\longrightarrow\widetilde M\otimes_{\mathcal O_U}\widetilde N.$$ [F1, F3, F5]

By [F2] the stalk of the tensor product of the associated sheaves is $$\bigl(\widetilde M\otimes_{\mathcal O_U}\widetilde N\bigr)_{\mathfrak p}\cong(\widetilde M)_{\mathfrak p}\otimes_{A_{\mathfrak p}}(\widetilde N)_{\mathfrak p}\cong M_{\mathfrak p}\otimes_{A_{\mathfrak p}}N_{\mathfrak p},$$ while by [F2] and [F3] the stalk of the associated tensor is $$\widetilde{(M\otimes_AN)}_{\mathfrak p}\cong(M\otimes_AN)_{\mathfrak p}\cong M_{\mathfrak p}\otimes_{A_{\mathfrak p}}N_{\mathfrak p}.$$ Under these identifications the map $\delta_{\mathfrak p}$ sends the class of $m\otimes n$ to the class of $m\otimes n$, and since the classes of the pure tensors generate both sides as $A_{\mathfrak p}$-modules, $\delta_{\mathfrak p}$ is the canonical isomorphism between the two copies of $M_{\mathfrak p}\otimes_{A_{\mathfrak p}}N_{\mathfrak p}$; in particular $\delta_{\mathfrak p}$ is bijective for every $\mathfrak p$. Exact localization and affine equivalence give coherent kernels, images, cokernels, finite sums and extensions. The Noetherian hypothesis is essential; zero objects and n=0 relation maps are covered. AC is inherited through QC interfaces.

boundaries.evidence: For $X=\varnothing$ every $\mathcal O_X$-module is the zero sheaf and the internal Hom is the zero sheaf, so the Definition applies vacuously and carries no quasi-coherence claim.

If $\mathcal F=0$ or $\mathcal G=0$ then $\mathcal H om(\mathcal F,\mathcal G)=0$: over $U$ the hom-set is that of maps from $0$ to $\mathcal G|_U$ or from $\mathcal F|_U$ to $0$, and both are the zero module, as recorded in the Definition.

For $\mathcal F=\mathcal G=\mathcal O_X$ the Definition gives sections $\mathcal O_X(U)$, i.e. $\mathcal H om(\mathcal O_X,\mathcal O_X)\cong\mathcal O_X$, matching the identification of endomorphisms of the structure sheaf with multiplication by global sections.

The degenerate behaviour recorded in the item: $\mathcal H om(\mathcal F,\mathcal G)_x$ is not $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_{X,x}}(\mathcal F_x,\mathcal G_x)$ in general, because a compatible family of local homomorphisms need not extend to a neighbourhood; only the natural comparison map from the stalk into the hom of stalks exists in one direction, exactly the warning recorded in the Definition.

boundaries.reason: The internal Hom has no interval, rank or endpoint parameter; the extremal cases are the zero module and the structure sheaf, recorded above.

boundaries.evidence: Sections are defined by the universal property $\Gamma(U,\mathcal H om(\mathcal F,\mathcal G))=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_U}(\mathcal F|_U,\mathcal G|_U)$ and gluing of homomorphisms is unique when it exists; no family of choices is made, the universal property fixed in the Definition.

Contravariance in $\mathcal F$: a morphism $\alpha:\mathcal F'\to\mathcal F$ induces precomposition $\alpha^*:\mathcal H om(\mathcal F,\mathcal G)\to\mathcal H om(\mathcal F',\mathcal G)$ on each open, which is $\mathcal O_X$-linear and compatible with restrictions, this is the contravariance asserted in the Definition.

Covariance and left exactness in $\mathcal G$: a morphism $\beta:\mathcal G\to\mathcal G'$ induces postcomposition, and for a short exact sequence $0\to\mathcal G'\to\mathcal G\to\mathcal G''$ the sequence of Hom sheaves is exact because $\operatorname{Hom}$ is left exact on each open and exactness of module sheaves is stalkwise, this is the covariance and left exactness asserted in the Definition.

derivations.claim: An affine chart where both sheaves are associated: let $x\in X$. By [F5] and the affine equivalence [F2] applied to an affine neighbourhood of $x$, and shrinking to a distinguished open inside the intersection of a chart for $\mathcal F$ and a chart for $\mathcal G$, there is an affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ containing $x$ with $\mathcal F|_U\cong\widetilde M$ and $\mathcal G|_U\cong\widetilde N$, where $M$ is finitely presented and $N$ is an arbitrary $A$-module; such charts cover $X$. [F2, F5]

Sections on distinguished opens: for $f\in A$, [F1] gives $\Gamma(D(f),\mathcal H om(\mathcal F,\mathcal G))=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_{D(f)}}(\mathcal F|_{D(f)},\mathcal G|_{D(f)})$, and by [F4] $\mathcal F|_{D(f)}=\widetilde{(M_f)}$ and $\mathcal G|_{D(f)}=\widetilde{(N_f)}$; since $D(f)$ is affine, [F2] identifies this Hom module canonically with $\operatorname{Hom}_{A_f}(M_f,N_f)$. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1]

The restriction maps are the localisation maps: for $D(g)\subseteq D(f)$ the restriction of a morphism of $\mathcal O_U$-modules is the map $\psi\mapsto\psi|_{D(g)}$, so under the identifications of step 2.1 the restriction $\Gamma(D(f),\mathcal H om)\to\Gamma(D(g),\mathcal H om)$ corresponds to $\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,N)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{A_f}(M_f,N_f)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{A_g}(M_g,N_g)$ obtained by functoriality of restriction of morphisms, which is exactly the composite of the natural localisation maps for $\operatorname{Hom}$; by [F3] this composite is the canonical localisation $\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,N)_f\to\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,N)_g$ under the identifications $\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,N)_f\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{A_f}(M_f,N_f)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,N)_g\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{A_g}(M_g,N_g)$, both isomorphisms because $M$ is finitely presented. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1]

The identification with the associated sheaf: by steps 2.1 and 3.1 the distinguished-open data of $\mathcal H om(\mathcal F,\mathcal G)|_U$ are the modules $\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,N)_f$, with restrictions the localisation maps, which are exactly the distinguished-open data of the associated sheaf $\widetilde{\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,N)}$; a morphism of $\mathcal O_U$-modules between these two sheaves is determined by its components on distinguished opens and a compatible family of isomorphisms on the basis extends uniquely, so the identity family assembles to a canonical isomorphism $\mathcal H om(\mathcal F,\mathcal G)|_U\cong\widetilde{\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,N)}$, natural in $M$ and $N$ because all identifications used are the canonical ones of [F1]–[F4]. This proves (2). [F2, F3, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1]

Claim 1 and claim 3: the charts $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ of step 1.1 cover $X$ and on each of them $\mathcal H om(\mathcal F,\mathcal G)|_U\cong\widetilde{\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,N)}$ is associated, so by the local form of the definition $\mathcal H om(\mathcal F,\mathcal G)$ is quasi-coherent, proving claim 1. On an overlap $U\cap U'$ of two such charts both isomorphisms are built from the restriction-of-morphisms identifications of the same sheaf $\mathcal H om(\mathcal F,\mathcal G)$, so they agree on the overlap: this is claim 3, and the canonical identifications restrict correctly on distinguished opens. [F1, step 4.1]

Choice accounting: no choice is used beyond the inherited Axiom of Choice of the affine equivalence [F2], which is used to identify Hom modules with Hom of associated sheaves; the localisation-of-Hom isomorphisms of [F3] are canonical, and all selections in step 1.1 involve finitely many charts around one point at a time. [F2, F3, step 4.1] ∎

boundaries.evidence: For $X=\varnothing$ the only sheaves are zero, so $\mathcal F=\mathcal G=0$ and $\mathcal H om(0,0)=0$ is quasi-coherent; the charts of step 1.1 do not exist and claims 2 and 3 are vacuous.

For $\mathcal F=0$ on a chart $M=0$ is finitely presented and $\operatorname{Hom}_A(0,N)=0=\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,N)$, so step 4.1 gives $\mathcal H om(0,\mathcal G)|_U=\widetilde 0=0$; for $\mathcal G=0$ similarly $\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,0)=0$, and the sheaf $\mathcal H om(\mathcal F,0)=0$ is quasi-coherent by step 5.1.

For $\mathcal F=\mathcal O_X$, so that $M=A$ on a chart, one has $\operatorname{Hom}_A(A,N)=N$ and step 4.1 identifies $\mathcal H om(\mathcal O_X,\mathcal G)|_U$ with $\widetilde N=\mathcal G|_U$, the expected untwisted case; $A$ is finitely presented as an $A$-module, and the localisation map in step 3.1 is the canonical isomorphism $N_f\to(N_f)$.

The degenerate cases in scope are a non-Noetherian base and an arbitrary, possibly non-finitely-generated $\mathcal G$: step 3.1 needs finite presentation of $M$ only, for $\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,N)_f\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{A_f}(M_f,N_f)$, and never finite generation of $N$; the case of $\mathcal F$ not finitely presented is deliberately excluded, as the Statement notes, since the localisation map of [F3] is only injective for finitely generated and can fail to be an isomorphism without finite presentation.

boundaries.reason: The Statement has no interval, degree, rank or numerical endpoint parameter: it is a local identification of sheaves, and the only extreme objects are $\mathcal F=0$ and $\mathcal G=0$, covered by the zero row, and $\mathcal F=\mathcal O_X$, covered by the one row.

boundaries.evidence: Step 6.1 records the accounting: the only Axiom of Choice used is the inherited one of the affine equivalence [F2]; the localisation-of-Hom isomorphisms of [F3] are canonical, and step 1.1 selects only finitely many charts around one point at a time.

Forward: $\mathcal H om(\mathcal F,\mathcal G)$ is quasi-coherent. The charts of step 1.1 cover $X$ and on each of them step 4.1 exhibits the restriction as an associated sheaf $\widetilde{\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,N)}$, so the local form of quasi-coherence is satisfied and step 5.1 concludes claim 1.

Reverse: on an affine chart with $\mathcal F|_U=\widetilde M$, $\mathcal G|_U=\widetilde N$ and $M$ finitely presented, the internal Hom is $\widetilde{\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,N)}$. Step 2.1 computes its sections on distinguished opens as $\operatorname{Hom}_{A_f}(M_f,N_f)$ and step 3.1 shows the restriction maps are exactly the localisation maps $\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,N)_f\to\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,N)_g$, so step 4.1 glues the basis data to the canonical isomorphism and step 5.1 adds compatibility on overlaps.

risk_review.notes: On a common affine chart, internal Hom sections on D(f) are Hom_{A_f}(M_f,N_f). Finite presentation of M makes Hom_A(M,N)_f→Hom_{A_f}(M_f,N_f) an isomorphism, compatible with restrictions; the resulting associated-sheaf charts prove quasi-coherence. The finite-presentation hypothesis is used exactly there, and AC is inherited from affine equivalence.

boundaries.evidence: At a point of a scheme the rank condition of the Definition is local; the empty scheme has no points, so the condition is vacuous, and the zero sheaf is locally free of rank $0$ on it.
Rank $0$ means $\mathcal E|_U\cong\mathcal O_U^0=0$, so a rank-zero locally free sheaf is the zero sheaf; conversely the zero sheaf satisfies the Definition with $r=0$.
Rank $1$ is the invertible case singled out in the Definition, and a single chart $U=X$ with $\mathcal E\cong\mathcal O_X$ satisfies it.

The Definition's well-definedness paragraph proves rank independence via invariant basis number over the nonzero local ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}$, so no degenerate chart can make $r(x)$ ambiguous; disconnected $X$ may carry different ranks.
The Definition's rank has boundary value $0$, treated explicitly: $\mathcal O_U^0=0$ and rank-zero sheaves are the zero sheaf.
The Definition is a local existence condition on charts and rank functions; it selects nothing beyond a chart at each point and uses no choice principle.
A locally free sheaf of rank $0$ vanishes on the members of an open cover, hence is the zero sheaf, as stated in the Definition's immediate consequences.
Conversely the zero sheaf is locally free of rank $0$ because $\mathcal O_U^0=0$ on every chart, as stated in the Definition's immediate consequences.

risk_review.notes: Checked local rank is independent of chart because nonzero local rings have invariant basis number; hence the rank function is locally constant and constant on connected components. Rank zero is exactly the zero sheaf, rank one gives the invertible case, and local free charts imply quasi-coherence via associated free modules. No global constant-rank claim is made.

derivations.claim: Cover criterion: if $\varphi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ is a morphism of $\mathcal O_Y$-modules and $Y=\bigcup_iW_i$ is an open cover such that each restriction $\varphi|_{W_i}:\mathcal F|_{W_i}\to\mathcal G|_{W_i}$ is an isomorphism, then $\varphi$ is an isomorphism; indeed injectivity is local by [F5], and for $t\in\mathcal G(V)$ the sections $s_i\in\mathcal F(V\cap W_i)$ with $\varphi(s_i)=t|_{V\cap W_i}$ agree on overlaps because $\varphi(s_i-s_j)=0$ and $\varphi$ is injective on $V\cap W_i\cap W_j$, so they glue by [F5] to $s\in\mathcal F(V)$ with $\varphi(s)=t$ by [F5] again. [F2, F5]

For every ringed space $(Z,\mathcal O_Z)$ and every $r\ge0$ the morphism $\alpha:\mathcal O_Z^{\,r}\to\mathcal H om_{\mathcal O_Z}(\mathcal O_Z^{\,r},\mathcal O_Z)$ that on sections over $V$ sends $(a_1,\dots,a_r)$ to the homomorphism $(x_1,\dots,x_r)\mapsto\sum_ix_ia_i$ is an isomorphism: its inverse sends $\psi\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_V}(\mathcal O_V^{\,r},\mathcal O_V)$ to $(\psi(e_1),\dots,\psi(e_r))$, where $e_1,\dots,e_r$ are the standard basis sections, and both maps are natural in $V$, so they define mutually inverse isomorphisms of sheaves; for $r=0$ both sides are the zero sheaf, since $\mathcal O_Z^0=0$ and $\operatorname{Hom}(0,\mathcal O_V)=0$, so the case of rank zero is included. [F2]

Let $\mathcal G$ be an $\mathcal O_X$-module and let $U\subseteq X$ be open, with $f_U:f^{-1}U\to U$ the restriction of $f$. Restricting the defining formula of [F3] to the open $f^{-1}U$ gives a canonical isomorphism $\rho:(f^*\mathcal G)|_{f^{-1}U}\to f_U^*(\mathcal G|_U)$, because $f^{-1}(\mathcal G|_U)=(f^{-1}\mathcal G)|_{f^{-1}U}$ and $\mathcal O_{f^{-1}U}=\mathcal O_Y|_{f^{-1}U}$; the isomorphisms $\rho$ are natural in $\mathcal G$ and in $U$: they are compatible with restrictions to smaller opens and with morphisms $u:\mathcal G\to\mathcal G'$. [F3]

Let $g:Z\to W$ be a morphism of ringed spaces and $r\ge0$: then there is a canonical isomorphism $g^*(\mathcal O_W^{\,r})\cong\mathcal O_Z^{\,r}$. Indeed, by [F3] $g^*(\mathcal O_W^{\,r})=\mathcal O_Z\otimes_{g^{-1}\mathcal O_W}g^{-1}(\mathcal O_W^{\,r})$; the inverse image of a finite direct sum is the direct sum of the inverse images, because on the colimit presheaf the construction is sectionwise and finite direct sums of presheaves are computed sectionwise, so $g^{-1}(\mathcal O_W^{\,r})=(g^{-1}\mathcal O_W)^r$; tensoring over the ring $g^{-1}\mathcal O_W$ distributes over finite direct sums and $\mathcal O_Z\otimes_{g^{-1}\mathcal O_W}g^{-1}\mathcal O_W\cong\mathcal O_Z$ because $g^{-1}\mathcal O_W\to\mathcal O_Z$ is a ring map making $\mathcal O_Z$ a module over $g^{-1}\mathcal O_W$ and tensoring a module by the ring itself returns the module; hence $g^*(\mathcal O_W^{\,r})\cong(\mathcal O_Z)^r$, with the case $r=0$ giving the zero sheaf. [F3]

Let $U\subseteq X$ be open with an isomorphism $\theta:\mathcal E|_U\to\mathcal O_U^{\,r}$. Then $\mathcal E^\vee|_U=\mathcal H om_{\mathcal O_X}(\mathcal E,\mathcal O_X)|_U \cong\mathcal H om_{\mathcal O_U}(\mathcal E|_U,\mathcal O_U) \cong\mathcal H om_{\mathcal O_U}(\mathcal O_U^{\,r},\mathcal O_U) \cong\mathcal O_U^{\,r}$, the first isomorphism by [F2], the second induced by $\theta$, and the last by step 1.2; hence $\mathcal E^\vee$ is finite locally free and agrees with $\mathcal E$ in rank on every chart. [F1, F2, step 1.2]

For each open $U\subseteq X$ define $\Psi_U:\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_U}(\mathcal E|_U,\mathcal O_U)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_{f^{-1}U}}(f^*\mathcal E|_{f^{-1}U},\mathcal O_{f^{-1}U})$ by $\varphi\mapsto\rho_{\mathcal O}^{-1}\circ f_U^*(\varphi)\circ\rho_{\mathcal E}$, where $\rho_{\mathcal E},\rho_{\mathcal O}$ are the isomorphisms of step 1.3 for $\mathcal G=\mathcal E$ and $\mathcal G=\mathcal O_X$; the maps $\Psi_U$ are compatible with restrictions in $U$ by the naturality of step 1.3, hence define a morphism of $\mathcal O_X$-modules $\Psi:\mathcal E^\vee\to f_*\mathcal H om_{\mathcal O_Y}(f^*\mathcal E,\mathcal O_Y)$; by the adjunction [F4] the morphism $\Psi$ has a transpose $$c:f^*(\mathcal E^\vee)\longrightarrow(f^*\mathcal E)^\vee,$$ the canonical comparison morphism, natural in $\mathcal E$ and $f$. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.3]

The evaluation morphism $\operatorname{ev}:\mathcal E\to\mathcal E^{\vee\vee}$ given on sections over $V$ by $e\mapsto(\varphi\mapsto\varphi(e))$ is well defined and $\mathcal O_X$-linear, because $\varphi\in\mathcal E^\vee(V)$ is a homomorphism $\mathcal E|_V\to\mathcal O_V$ by [F2] and the assignment is additive and $\mathcal O_V$-linear in $e$ and compatible with restrictions; on a chart $U$ of step 2.1 with trivialization $\theta$ and basis $e_1,\dots,e_r$ of $\mathcal E|_U$ mapping to the standard basis, the dual basis $\varphi_j=\theta_j$ of $\mathcal E^\vee|_U$ satisfies $\operatorname{ev}(e_j)(\varphi)=\varphi(e_j)$, so under the identifications $\mathcal E^\vee|_U\cong\mathcal O_U^{\,r}$ and $\mathcal E^{\vee\vee}|_U\cong\mathcal O_U^{\,r}$ supplied by step 1.2 the map $\operatorname{ev}|_U$ corresponds to the identity matrix and is an isomorphism; by the cover criterion of step 1.1 applied to a trivialising cover of $X$, $\operatorname{ev}$ is an isomorphism. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2]

Let $U\subseteq X$ be a chart of $\mathcal E$ as in step 2.1. On $f^{-1}U$ the morphism $c$ is computed by steps 1.3 and 1.2 as follows: the identifications $f^*(\mathcal E^\vee)|_{f^{-1}U}\cong f_U^*(\mathcal E^\vee|_U) \cong f_U^*(\mathcal O_U^{\,r})\cong\mathcal O_{f^{-1}U}^{\,r}$ and $(f^*\mathcal E)^\vee|_{f^{-1}U}\cong\mathcal H om_{\mathcal O_{f^{-1}U}}(f_U^*(\mathcal E|_U),\mathcal O_{f^{-1}U}) \cong\mathcal H om_{\mathcal O_{f^{-1}U}}(\mathcal O_{f^{-1}U}^{\,r},\mathcal O_{f^{-1}U}) \cong\mathcal O_{f^{-1}U}^{\,r}$ hold by step 1.4 and steps 1.3, 1.2, and the transpose construction of step 2.2 sends the pulled-back $j$-th basis functional $\varphi_j$ — a local section of $f^*(\mathcal E^\vee)$ — to $f_U^*(\varphi_j)$, which under these identifications is the $j$-th coordinate functional of $\mathcal O_{f^{-1}U}^{\,r}$, that is, the $j$-th basis element; therefore $c|_{f^{-1}U}$ corresponds to the identity matrix and is an isomorphism. [step 1.2, step 1.4, step 2.2]

Choosing a trivialising open cover of $X$, the opens $f^{-1}U$ cover $Y$ and $c$ restricts to an isomorphism on each of them by step 3.2, so $c$ is an isomorphism by the cover criterion of step 1.1: this proves claim 3, while claim 1 is step 2.1 and claim 2 is step 3.1. Every morphism constructed is canonical and all identifications involve only finitely many standard basis elements of a free module of finite rank, so no choice principle is used. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2] ∎

boundaries.evidence: For $X=\varnothing$ the sheaf $\mathcal E$ is the zero sheaf, the case $r=0$ of step 1.2, and $\mathcal E^\vee=0$ with $\operatorname{ev}$ the identity of the zero sheaf; the Statement holds vacuously and every claim is trivial.

For $\mathcal E=0$ step 1.2 with $r=0$ gives $\mathcal E^\vee=0$, hence $\mathcal E^{\vee\vee}=0$, and $\operatorname{ev}$ is the zero map between zero sheaves, an isomorphism in step 3.1; step 1.3 gives $f^*0=0=(f^*0)^\vee$.

For $\mathcal E=\mathcal O_X$ step 1.2 identifies $\mathcal E^\vee\cong\mathcal O_X$ by $a\mapsto(x\mapsto xa)$, and under this identification $\operatorname{ev}$ of step 3.1 is the identity, so claims 1 and 2 hold with rank one everywhere.

The degenerate case is a non-connected $X$ on which the rank of $\mathcal E$ varies: step 2.1 computes $\mathcal E^\vee|_U\cong\mathcal O_U^{\,r}$ on each chart, so the rank function of $\mathcal E^\vee$ equals that of $\mathcal E$ without any global constancy assumption, and step 3.2 covers the rank-zero charts through $r=0$.

boundaries.reason: The Statement has no interval, degree or endpoint parameter; the extremal ranks $r=0$ and $r=1$ are covered by the zero and one rows.

The canonical maps of the Statement are constructed in steps 2.2 and 3.1: the comparison $c$ as the transpose of pulling back homomorphisms, and $\operatorname{ev}$ by evaluation, both without arbitrary choices.

The inverse directions are supplied by the local computations: $\operatorname{ev}$ is an isomorphism by step 3.1 restricted to a trivialising cover and the cover criterion of step 1.1, and $c$ is an isomorphism by the local computation of step 3.2 together with step 4.1.

risk_review.notes: Checked on a rank-r trivializing chart the internal Hom of O^r with O is O^r, evaluation is the identity matrix, and pullback commutes with finite free duals; the canonical comparison isomorphism is local on the pullback cover. Rank zero and locally varying finite rank are included; no choice principle is used.

boundaries.evidence: The Definition permits X to be empty: its only affine chart is Spec(0), all gluing conditions are vacuous, and Sym(0)=O_X with degree-zero part O_X.

For the zero module $\mathcal F=0$ every affine model has $M=0$, and $\operatorname{Sym}_A(0)=A$ concentrated in degree zero because the tensor algebra of the zero module is $A$ in degree zero; hence $\operatorname{Sym}(0)=\mathcal O_X$, consistent with $\operatorname{Sym}^0=\mathcal O_X$ and $\operatorname{Sym}^1=0$. The zero module and the zero ring are not excluded by the Definition.

For $\mathcal F=\mathcal O_X$ the affine model of the Definition is $M=A$, and $\operatorname{Sym}_A(A)=A[T]$ is the polynomial algebra on one degree-one generator, so $\operatorname{Sym}(\mathcal O_X)\cong\mathcal O_X[T]=\bigoplus_{d\ge0}\mathcal O_X\cdot T^d$ with $\operatorname{Sym}^1=\mathcal O_X$; this is the case $r=1$ of the model $\operatorname{Sym}_A(A^r)=A[T_1,\dots,T_r]$ stated in the Definition.

Degenerate inputs are allowed by the Definition and accounted for: the zero ring $A=0$ occurs when an admissible chart $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ is empty, where $\operatorname{Sym}_A(M)$ is the zero ring and the associated sheaf on $\varnothing$ is the zero sheaf; the degrees $d=0$ and $d=1$ are the degenerate grading cases $\operatorname{Sym}^0=\mathcal O_X$ and $\operatorname{Sym}^1=\mathcal F$; and no finiteness hypothesis (Noetherian, finitely generated, separated or locally free) is imposed on $\mathcal F$, $X$ or $M$.

The grading has the two endpoint degrees $d=0$ and $d=1$: $\operatorname{Sym}^0(\mathcal F)=\mathcal O_X$ is the unit and $\operatorname{Sym}^1(\mathcal F)=\mathcal F$ is the degree-one part; the multiplication maps $\operatorname{Sym}^d\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^e\to\operatorname{Sym}^{d+e}$ at $d=0$ or $e=0$ are the unit isomorphisms of the algebra, and there is no other interval, rank or degree parameter in the Definition.

The Definition constructs the cover from all admissible affine opens and uses the canonical module Gamma(U,F) and canonical base-change maps. Its opening AC premise is inherited from associated-sheaf existence and affine quasi-coherent equivalence; this gluing makes no new simultaneous choices.

Forward (well-definedness of the local models in the Definition): for affine $V=\operatorname{Spec}C\subseteq U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ with $\mathcal F|_U\cong\widetilde M$ one has $\mathcal F|_V\cong\widetilde{(C\otimes_AM)}$ and the base-change isomorphism $\operatorname{Sym}_A(M)\otimes_AC\cong\operatorname{Sym}_C(M\otimes_AC)$, which together with the natural restriction isomorphism $(\widetilde N)|_V\cong\widetilde{(C\otimes_AN)}$ gives the canonical isomorphism $\theta_{U,V}:\operatorname{Sym}_U|_V\cong\operatorname{Sym}_V$ satisfying the cocycle identity on triples.

Reverse (determination by the models of the Definition): a sheaf is determined by its restrictions to a cover together with overlap identifications, so the glued sheaf $\operatorname{Sym}(\mathcal F)$ restricts back to $\operatorname{Sym}_U$ on every admissible affine open $U$ and is unique up to unique isomorphism among sheaves with these restrictions; in particular the affine model $\operatorname{Sym}(\mathcal F)|_U\cong(\operatorname{Sym}_A(M))^{\sim}$ is recovered, as stated in the Affine model paragraph of the Definition.

risk_review.notes: Checked tensor algebra quotient by homogeneous commutators, Sym^0=A and Sym^1=M, permutation relations and the free-rank-r polynomial case. Base-change maps on affine restrictions preserve grading and satisfy cocycles, so the glued algebra and its universal property are well defined. Empty and rank-zero cases give O_X; AC is inherited from associated-sheaf machinery and affine equivalence (including compactness of Spec A). Choice accounting corrected by step7-v2-repeat-r1-u7; this correction is not an independent review of its own repair.

derivations.claim: Universal property of the affine model: for a commutative ring $A$, an $A$-module $M$ and a commutative $A$-algebra $C$, the map $g\mapsto g\circ\eta$ induced by the degree-one inclusion $\eta:M\to\operatorname{Sym}_A(M)$ is a bijection $A\text{-}\mathrm{Alg}(\operatorname{Sym}_A(M),C)\to\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,C)$: apply the universal property of [F1] on $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$ to $\mathcal F=\widetilde M$ and the sheaf of commutative $\mathcal O_X$-algebras $\widetilde C$, and translate along the affine equivalence [F2], under which $\mathcal O_X$-linear maps $\widetilde M\to\widetilde C$ are the $A$-linear maps $M\to C$, while $\operatorname{Sym}(\widetilde M)\cong(\operatorname{Sym}_A(M))^{\sim}$ by the affine model of [F1] and the tensor identifications [F3] match the multiplications, so $\mathcal O_X$-algebra maps $\operatorname{Sym}(\widetilde M)\to\widetilde C$ are the $A$-algebra maps $\operatorname{Sym}_A(M)\to C$; the bijection is natural in $C$ because the equivalence and the universal property are. [F1, F2, F3]

2.1 Base change of the affine model: for a ring map $A\to B$ and an $A$-module $M$ there is a canonical isomorphism of graded $B$-algebras $\beta:B\otimes_A\operatorname{Sym}_A(M)\to\operatorname{Sym}_B(B\otimes_AM)$ characterized by $\beta(1\otimes\eta_A(m))=\eta_B(1\otimes m)$: both sides represent the same functor of commutative $B$-algebras, since [F6] identifies $B$-algebra maps $B\otimes_A\operatorname{Sym}_A(M)\to D$ with $A$-algebra maps $\operatorname{Sym}_A(M)\to D$, step 1.1 with $A$-linear maps $M\to D$, [F6] with $B$-linear maps $B\otimes_AM\to D$, and step 1.1 over $B$ with $B$-algebra maps $\operatorname{Sym}_B(B\otimes_AM)\to D$; the identity of $\operatorname{Sym}_B(B\otimes_AM)$ corresponds to a map $\beta$ and the identity of $B\otimes_A\operatorname{Sym}_A(M)$ to a map $\gamma$, and naturality in $D$ gives $\beta\circ\gamma=\mathrm{id}$ and $\gamma\circ\beta=\mathrm{id}$. Under this correspondence $\beta$ is the unique $B$-algebra map with $\beta(1\otimes\eta_A(m))=\eta_B(1\otimes m)$, so it preserves the degree-one generators and hence the grading, and for $A\to B\to C$ both composites $C\otimes_A\operatorname{Sym}_A(M)\to\operatorname{Sym}_C(C\otimes_AM)$ in the claim are $C$-algebra maps sending $1\otimes\eta_A(m)$ to $\eta_C(1\otimes m)$; since the source is generated as a $C$-algebra by these elements, the composites agree, the identifications $C\otimes_B(B\otimes_AN)\cong C\otimes_AN$ being those of [F6]. [F6, step 1.1]

Restriction to open subschemes: for an open subscheme $W\subseteq X$ there is a canonical isomorphism of graded $\mathcal O_W$-algebras $\operatorname{Sym}(\mathcal F)|_W\cong\operatorname{Sym}(\mathcal F|_W)$, compatible with inclusions $W'\subseteq W$: the affine opens $U=\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq W$ with $\mathcal F|_U\cong\widetilde M$ cover $W$ because $\mathcal F$ is quasi-coherent, and on each of them $\operatorname{Sym}(\mathcal F)|_U\cong(\operatorname{Sym}_A(M))^{\sim}$ by the affine model, while applying the same model to the quasi-coherent sheaf $\mathcal F|_W$ on $W$ gives $\operatorname{Sym}(\mathcal F|_W)|_U\cong(\operatorname{Sym}_A(M))^{\sim}$ with the same module $M=\Gamma(U,\mathcal F)$; for affine $U'\subseteq U$ both identifications restrict by the canonical base-change isomorphism of step 2.1 for the ring map $\Gamma(U,\mathcal O)\to\Gamma(U',\mathcal O)$, so the chartwise isomorphisms agree on overlaps and glue by [F5] to a graded $\mathcal O_W$-algebra isomorphism, and passing to the subcover inside $W'\subseteq W$ shows compatibility with inclusions. [F1, F5, step 2.1]

3.2 Pullback along an arbitrary morphism: for $f:Y\to X$ there is a canonical isomorphism of graded $\mathcal O_Y$-algebras $f^*\operatorname{Sym}(\mathcal F)\cong\operatorname{Sym}(f^*\mathcal F)$: cover $Y$ by affine opens $V=\operatorname{Spec}B$ with $f(V)\subseteq U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ for an affine $U\subseteq X$ on which $\mathcal F|_U\cong\widetilde M$, which is possible because affine opens form a basis and $\mathcal F$ is quasi-coherent; on such $V$ the affine form of the pullback [F4] applied to $\mathcal F$ and to the quasi-coherent $\operatorname{Sym}(\mathcal F)$ gives $f^*\mathcal F|_V\cong\widetilde{(B\otimes_AM)}$ and $f^*\operatorname{Sym}(\mathcal F)|_V\cong\widetilde{(B\otimes_A\operatorname{Sym}_A(M))}$, while the affine model [F1] applied to the quasi-coherent $f^*\mathcal F$ on $V$ gives $\operatorname{Sym}(f^*\mathcal F)|_V\cong(\operatorname{Sym}_B\Gamma(V,f^*\mathcal F))^{\sim}=(\operatorname{Sym}_B(B\otimes_AM))^{\sim}$ using $\Gamma(V,\widetilde{(B\otimes_AM)})=B\otimes_AM$ [F2]; the base-change isomorphism $\beta$ of step 2.1 is a graded $\mathcal O_V$-algebra isomorphism between these two models, and on an affine $V'\subseteq V$ the two restrictions agree because $\beta$ is compatible with the ring map $B\to\Gamma(V',\mathcal O)$ by step 2.1, on overlaps from different target charts they also agree: both send each local pulled-back degree-one section to its degree-one image, and such sections generate the source algebra. Thus the local isomorphisms glue over the cover of $Y$ by [F5] to a canonical isomorphism which is graded and multiplicative because the local ones are. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 2.1]

The remaining claims: $\operatorname{Sym}(\mathcal F)$ is a quasi-coherent graded commutative $\mathcal O_X$-algebra with $\operatorname{Sym}^0(\mathcal F)=\mathcal O_X$ and $\operatorname{Sym}^1(\mathcal F)=\mathcal F$, and for $\mathcal F=\mathcal O_X^{\,r}$ it is $\mathcal O_X[T_1,\dots,T_r]$ with $\deg T_i=1$, by the affine models of [F1]; the base-change isomorphism of step 2.1 for $M=A^r$ gives the same polynomial algebra after extension of scalars, so the two descriptions are consistent. Over a nonempty $X$ the empty total space is excluded, which the Definition records through the normalised grading $\mathcal A_0=\mathcal O_X\neq0$, matching that the rank-zero bundle over nonempty $X$ is $X$ itself, not $\varnothing$.

Rank zero is treated in the Definition: a rank-zero geometric vector bundle has $\mathcal A_1=0$, hence $\mathcal A=\mathcal A_0=\mathcal O_X$ and $V=X$; conversely $\mathbb V(0)=\operatorname{Spec}_X\operatorname{Sym}(0)=\operatorname{Spec}_X\mathcal O_X=X$, the bundle with one zero vector over every point of $X$.

Rank one occurs as the trivialization $\mathcal A|_U\cong\operatorname{Sym}(\mathcal O_U^1)=\mathcal O_U[T_1]$ of the Definition, and $\mathbb V(\mathcal O_X)\cong\mathbf A^1_X$ is the trivial line bundle; the rank function of the Definition assigns the value $1$ on the whole chart, the invertible case of [[def-locally-free-sheaf-finite-rank]].

The Definition excludes the two degenerate readings: a 'grading' is required to be normalised, $\mathcal A_0=\mathcal O_X$, so the empty total space over nonempty $X$ (with relative coordinate algebra $0$ and no such grading) is not a geometric vector bundle; and the local triviality condition forces the degree-one part $\mathcal A_1$ to be locally free, so a grading with non-locally-free $\mathcal A_1$ is not admitted. The Definition's rank parameter runs over $\mathbb N$ with endpoint $0$ treated explicitly: $r=0$ gives $\operatorname{Sym}(\mathcal O_U^0)=\mathcal O_U$ and $\mathbb V(0)=X$. The grading itself has the endpoint $d=0$ fixed as $\mathcal A_0=\mathcal O_X$, while the degree-one part generates.

The Definition's Choice paragraph records that the data of a geometric vector bundle are a scheme morphism together with a grading, and that the construction of $\mathbb V(\mathcal E)$ uses the family of all affine opens trivializing $\mathcal E$ without selecting a chart or an isomorphism; the only Axiom of Choice is the inherited one used by [[lem-relative-spec-glues-affine-algebras]] and [[lem-symmetric-algebra-qc-and-base-change]]. The finite locally free $\mathcal O_X$-modules with $\mathcal O_X$-linear maps form a category, and a finite locally free $\mathcal O_X$-module is quasi-coherent with a well-defined locally constant rank by [F2]; the geometric vector bundles over $X$ with the morphisms of [F1] form a category by [F1] and [F13]. Chart dictionary. Let $(V,\mathcal A)$ be a geometric vector bundle with structure morphism $\pi_V$, let $U=\operatorname{Spec}R\subseteq X$ be affine with a graded isomorphism $\mathcal A|_U\cong\operatorname{Sym}(\mathcal O_U^r)$ of the bundle data, and let $D(s)\subseteq U$ be a principal open; then $\pi_V^{-1}(U)\cong\operatorname{Spec}\Gamma(U,\mathcal A) \cong\operatorname{Spec}R[T_1,\dots,T_r]=\mathbf A^r_U$ as $U$-schemes, the chart of $D(s)$ is the restriction with transition the localization $R[T_1,\dots,T_r]\to R[T_1,\dots,T_r]_s$, and the degree-one part is $\mathcal A_1|_U\cong\mathcal O_U^r$. For the total space of a finite locally free $\mathcal E$ the same chart reads $\pi^{-1}(U)\cong\operatorname{Spec}\Gamma(U,\operatorname{Sym}(\mathcal E^\vee))\cong\operatorname{Spec}R[T_1,\dots,T_r]$ whenever $\mathcal E|_U\cong\mathcal O_U^r$. [F1, F3, F4, F5, F6, F8]

The functor $\Phi$. For a geometric vector bundle $(V,\mathcal A)$ the degree-one part $\mathcal A_1$ is finite locally free of rank equal to the rank of the bundle by [F1] and [F2]; put $\Phi(V,\mathcal A):=\mathcal A_1^\vee$, finite locally free of the same rank by [F3]. For a morphism $\varphi:(V,\mathcal A)\to(W,\mathcal B)$ with graded comorphism $\varphi^\sharp:\mathcal B\to\mathcal A$, put $\Phi(\varphi):=(\varphi^\sharp_1)^\vee:\mathcal A_1^\vee\to\mathcal B_1^\vee$, an $\mathcal O_X$-linear map of finite locally free modules [F3]. Identities and composites are preserved: $\Phi(\mathrm{id})=\mathrm{id}$, and for a second morphism $\omega:(W,\mathcal B)\to(Z,\mathcal C)$ one has $(\omega\circ\varphi)^\sharp_1=\varphi^\sharp_1\circ\omega^\sharp_1$, whose transpose is $(\omega^\sharp_1)^\vee\circ(\varphi^\sharp_1)^\vee= \Phi(\omega)\circ\Phi(\varphi)$. Hence $\Phi$ is a covariant functor $\operatorname{GVB}(X)\to\operatorname{FLF}(X)$ preserving ranks. [F1, F2, F3, F13]

Induced morphism from a graded algebra map. Let $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$ be graded $\mathcal O_X$-algebras that are locally polynomial in the sense that their relative coordinate algebras admit the charts of step 1.2 for the same covering opens; then every graded $\mathcal O_X$-algebra map $\psi:\mathcal B\to\mathcal A$ induces an $X$-morphism $\Psi(\psi):\operatorname{Spec}_X\mathcal A\to \operatorname{Spec}_X\mathcal B$ with comorphism $\psi$. Construction: cover $X$ by the affine opens $U=\operatorname{Spec}R$ over which both algebras are graded free of ranks $s$ and $r$; the global sections map $\psi(U):R[T_1,\dots,T_s]\to R[T_1,\dots,T_r]$ is an $R$-algebra map by [F10] under the chart identifications of [F6], giving the $U$-morphism $\operatorname{Spec}(\psi(U))$ between the charts by [F9]. These chart morphisms glue: for a principal open $D(t)\subseteq U$ the restriction of $\psi(U)$ is $\psi(D(t))$ by [F10], so $\operatorname{Spec}(\psi(D(t)))$ is the restriction of $\operatorname{Spec}(\psi(U))$ to the subchart by [F8] and [F9]; hence all chart morphisms agree on overlaps after refining by affine opens, and they glue to an $X$-morphism $\Psi(\psi)$ because the source is covered by the charts and its structure sheaf is a sheaf [F11]. The comorphism of $\Psi(\psi)$ restricts to $\psi(U)$ on each chart, whence it equals $\psi$ [F10, F11]. [F4, F5, F6, F8, F9, F10, F11, F12]

Minors detect the rank drop: for a given $r\ge0$ and $s=n-r$, the inequality $\operatorname{rank}(\varphi\otimes\kappa(\mathfrak p))<s$ holds if and only if all $s\times s$ minors of the reduced matrix vanish, which happens if and only if every $s\times s$ minor of the matrix of $\varphi$ lies in $\mathfrak p$, that is, $I_{n-r}(\varphi)\subseteq\mathfrak p$; the conventions of [F1] give $I_{n-r}(\varphi)=A$ when $s\le0$, and $\operatorname{rank}<s$ is then impossible, while for $s>n$ one has $I_{n-r}(\varphi)=0$ and $\operatorname{rank}<s$ holds always. The rank locus on a chart: combining steps 1.1 and 2.1, for $\mathfrak p\in U$ one has $\dim_{\kappa(\mathfrak p)}\mathcal F(\mathfrak p)>r$ if and only if $I_{n-r}(\varphi)\subseteq\mathfrak p$; by [F1] the stalk of $\operatorname{Fitt}_r(\mathcal F)$ at $\mathfrak p$ is $I_{n-r}(\varphi)\cdot A_{\mathfrak p}$, and $I\cdot A_{\mathfrak p}\subseteq\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}$ if and only if $I\subseteq\mathfrak p$; hence $\mathfrak p\in V(\operatorname{Fitt}_r(\mathcal F))$ if and only if $\dim_{\kappa(\mathfrak p)}\mathcal F(\mathfrak p)>r$. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1]

Converse, the case $n=r$: let $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ be affine with $\mathcal F|_U\cong\widetilde M$, presentation $A^{(J)}\xrightarrow{\varphi}A^n\to M\to0$, and assume $I_{n-r}(\varphi)=A$, $I_{n-r+1}(\varphi)=0$ for some $r\ge1$. If $A=0$ the conclusion is vacuous, so assume $A\neq0$; then $n\ge r$, since $n-r+1\le0$ would force $A=I_{n-r+1}(\varphi)=0$. If $n=r$, then $I_1(\varphi)=I_{n-r+1}(\varphi)=0$ says that every entry of the matrix of $\varphi$ is zero, so $\varphi=0$ and $M=\operatorname{coker}\varphi\cong A^n=A^r$ is free of rank $r$. [F1, step 2.1]

Claim 1 globally: the affine charts of step 3.1 cover $X$ by [F2] and the assertion is pointwise in each chart, so $V(\operatorname{Fitt}_r(\mathcal F))=\{x:\dim_{\kappa(x)}\mathcal F(x)>r\}$ and $D(\operatorname{Fitt}_r(\mathcal F))$ is its complement $\{x:\dim_{\kappa(x)}\mathcal F(x)\le r\}$; this proves claim 1. Converse, the case $n>r$: keep the hypotheses of step 3.2 with $s=n-r\ge1$. The $s\times s$ minors of $\varphi$ generate $I_s(\varphi)=A$, so the distinguished opens $D(\delta)\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}A$, as $\delta$ runs over the $s\times s$ minors, cover $\operatorname{Spec}A$; fix such a minor $\delta$ and invert it. Over $A_\delta$ the selected minor is a unit, so after permuting the $s$ chosen rows and columns into the top-left corner, row operations by invertible $n\times n$ matrices and column operations by an automorphism of $A_\delta^{(J)}$ put the matrix of $\varphi\otimes A_\delta$ into block form $\begin{pmatrix}I_s&0\\ C&\psi\end{pmatrix}$ with $\psi$ of size $r$ rows; the $(s+1)\times(s+1)$ minors formed from $s$ rows and $s$ columns of the identity block together with one further row and column are, up to sign, exactly the entries of $\psi$, and they vanish because $I_{s+1}(\varphi)\otimes A_\delta=I_{n-r+1}(\varphi)\otimes A_\delta=0$; hence $\psi=0$ and $M_\delta\cong\operatorname{coker}\begin{pmatrix}I_s&0\\ C&0\end{pmatrix}\cong A_\delta^{\,r}$, because the image is the graph $\{(x,Cx)\}$, a direct summand of $A_\delta^n$ of rank $s$. Thus $\mathcal F$ is free of rank $r$ on each member $D(\delta)$ of a cover of $U$, so $\mathcal F|_U$ is locally free of rank $r$. [F1, F9, step 3.2]

Claim 2, the support: taking $r=0$ in claim 1 gives $V(\operatorname{Fitt}_0(\mathcal F))=\{x:\dim_{\kappa(x)}\mathcal F(x)>0\}=\{x:\mathcal F(x)
eq0\}$. For finite type $\mathcal F$ one has $\mathcal F(x)=0$ only if $\mathcal F$ vanishes on a neighbourhood of $x$, hence only if $\mathcal F_x=0$, and conversely $\mathcal F_x=0$ gives $\mathcal F(x)=0$; therefore $\{x:\mathcal F(x)
eq0\}=\{x:\mathcal F_x
eq0\}=\operatorname{Supp}(\mathcal F)$, and this agrees with the closedness of the support in [F5]. [F4, F5, step 4.1]

Claim 3, the locally free case: suppose $\mathcal F$ is finite locally free of rank $r$, so that by [F2] $X$ is covered by affine opens $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ with $\mathcal F|_U\cong\mathcal O_U^r=\widetilde{A^r}$; for the presentation $A^r=A^r$ with $n=r$ generators and no relations the matrix has $r$ rows and $0$ columns, so by the conventions of [F1] $I_{r-k}(\varphi)=A$ for $k\ge r$ and $I_{r-k}(\varphi)=0$ for $0\le k<r$, whence $\operatorname{Fitt}_k(\mathcal F)|_U=\mathcal O_U$ for $k\ge r$ and $=0$ for $k<r$; in particular $\operatorname{Fitt}_{r-1}(\mathcal F)|_U=0$ and $\operatorname{Fitt}_r(\mathcal F)|_U=\mathcal O_U$ for every member of a cover of $X$, and since membership in an ideal subsheaf and the equality with $\mathcal O_X$ are checked on a cover, $\operatorname{Fitt}_{r-1}(\mathcal F)=0$ and $\operatorname{Fitt}_r(\mathcal F)=\mathcal O_X$. [F1, F2, step 4.1]

Claim 4 globally: let $U\subseteq X$ be open with $\operatorname{Fitt}_{r-1}(\mathcal F)|_U=0$ and $\operatorname{Fitt}_r(\mathcal F)|_U=\mathcal O_U$. If $r=0$, claim 1 gives $\dim_{\kappa(x)}\mathcal F(x)\le0$, hence $\mathcal F(x)=0$, for every $x\in U$, and [F4] then shows that $\mathcal F$ vanishes on a neighbourhood of every point of $U$, so that $\mathcal F|_U=0$ is locally free of rank $0$. If $r\ge1$, cover $U$ by affine charts $V=\operatorname{Spec}A$ with $\mathcal F|_V\cong\widetilde M$; on each chart the restriction of the hypotheses reads $I_{n-r}(\varphi)=A$ and $I_{n-r+1}(\varphi)=0$ by [F1], so steps 3.2 and 4.2 show that $\mathcal F|_V$ is free of rank $r$ on the members of a cover of $V$; these covers for all charts combine to a cover of $U$ by opens on which $\mathcal F$ is free of rank $r$. This proves claim 4. [F1, F2, F4, step 3.2, step 4.2]

Claim 5, sharpness: let $k$ be a field, $A=k[t]/(t^2)$ with class $\varepsilon$ of $t$, so that $\varepsilon^2=0$ and $\varepsilon\neq0$, and let $M=A/(\varepsilon)=k$; then $M$ is generated by one element with the single relation $\varepsilon\cdot1=0$, giving a presentation $A\xrightarrow{\ \varepsilon\ }A\to M\to0$, and $\mathcal F=\widetilde M$ is a finite type quasi-coherent module on $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$, whose underlying space is the single point $\mathfrak p=(\varepsilon)$. The fibre there is $\mathcal F(\mathfrak p)=M\otimes_A\kappa(\mathfrak p)=M/\varepsilon M=k$, of dimension $1$ over $\kappa(\mathfrak p)=k$; the Fitting ideals of this presentation are $\operatorname{Fitt}_0(M)=I_1(\varphi)=(\varepsilon)\neq A$ and $\operatorname{Fitt}_1(M)=I_0(\varphi)=A$. Conclusion and choice accounting: claims 1 and 2 are steps 4.1 and 5.1, claim 3 is step 5.2, claim 4 is step 5.3 and claim 5 is step 6.1. All constructions are local and finite: a presentation with finitely many generators is used on one affine chart at a time, the minors of a matrix are indexed by finite subsets of that presentation, and the cover $\{D(\delta)\}$ in step 4.2 is the set of all distinguished opens defined by the minors, so no selection of points, presentations or minors is made; the only use of the Axiom of Choice is the one inherited from the associated-sheaf machinery through [F1] and [F5], and no Noetherian hypothesis is used, exactly as claimed. [F1, F5, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 5.2, step 5.3, step 6.1] ∎

derivations.claim: An ideal sheaf on an affine chart is associated to its global sections: let $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ be an affine open and let $\mathcal I\subseteq\mathcal O_X$ be a quasi-coherent ideal sheaf; put $J=\Gamma(U,\mathcal I)$, which is an ideal of $A=\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_X)$ because $\mathcal I$ is an ideal in every section ring. By [F1] applied to the quasi-coherent module $\mathcal I|_U$, the canonical comparison $\widetilde J\to\mathcal I|_U$ is an isomorphism, and naturality of the comparison with respect to the inclusion $\mathcal I\subseteq\mathcal O_X$ shows that it is an isomorphism of subsheaves of $\mathcal O_U=\widetilde A$; hence $\mathcal I|_U=\widetilde J$ and, by [F2], the stalk criterion $\mathcal I_{\mathfrak p}\neq\mathcal O_{U,\mathfrak p}$ holds exactly for $\mathfrak p\in V(J)$, so $V(\mathcal I)\cap U=V(J)$ and $V(\mathcal I)$ is closed in $X$ because the affine charts cover $X$. [F1, F2]

The kernel of a closed immersion is a quasi-coherent ideal sheaf: let $i:Z\to X$ be a closed immersion and put $K=\ker(\mathcal O_X\to i_*\mathcal O_Z)$, computed as a kernel of sheaves, so that $K$ is a subsheaf of $\mathcal O_X$ and an ideal in every section ring. Let $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ be an affine open of $X$; by the batch-5 supplier [F6] there is an ideal $J\subseteq A$ with $i^{-1}(U)\cong\operatorname{Spec}(A/J)$ and with $i|_U$ the quotient map, so over $U$ the structure map is $\widetilde A\to\widetilde{A/J}$ and [F2] identifies its kernel with $\widetilde J$; hence $K|_U=\widetilde J$ is associated, and because the affine charts cover $X$ the ideal sheaf $K$ satisfies the local definition of quasi-coherence. The uniqueness of $J$ in [F6] shows in addition that the local descriptions agree on overlaps, so $K$ is well defined independently of the charts. This is the exact point where the batch-5 supplier is consumed. [F2, F6]

The affine model of the construction: with $J=\Gamma(U,\mathcal I)$ as in step 1.1, [F2] identifies the quotient $\mathcal O_U/\mathcal I|_U=\mathcal O_U/\widetilde J$ with $\widetilde{A/J}$, and [F3] identifies $\operatorname{Spec}(A/J)$ with the closed subset $V(J)$; the sections of both structure sheaves on the distinguished open $D(\bar f)\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}(A/J)$ corresponding to $D(f)\cap V(J)$ are $(A/J)_f=A_f/J_f$, so the locally ringed space $(V(J),(\mathcal O_U/\widetilde J)|_{V(J)})$ is isomorphic to the affine scheme $\operatorname{Spec}(A/J)$. Consequently every point of $V(\mathcal I)$ has an open neighbourhood in the closed ringed subspace $Z_{\mathcal I}=(V(\mathcal I),(\mathcal O_X/\mathcal I)|_{V(\mathcal I)})$ isomorphic to an affine scheme, and by [F5] the space $Z_{\mathcal I}$ is a scheme. [F2, F3, F5, step 1.1]

The closed immersion is recovered from its kernel: with $K=K_Z$ as in step 1.2, the map $\mathcal O_X\to i_*\mathcal O_Z$ is surjective by the definition of a closed immersion, so it induces an isomorphism of sheaves of rings $\mathcal O_X/K\cong i_*\mathcal O_Z$; moreover $V(K)=\{x:K_x\neq\mathcal O_{X,x}\}=\{x:(i_*\mathcal O_Z)_x\neq0\}$ because $K_x$ is the kernel of the surjection $\mathcal O_{X,x}\to(i_*\mathcal O_Z)_x$, and this set is the image of $i$: for $x=i(z)$ the stalk $(i_*\mathcal O_Z)_x$ is the local ring $\mathcal O_{Z,z}$, which is nonzero for every point of a scheme, while for $x$ outside the closed image the stalk is $0$. Hence the canonical map $Z\to Z_{K}$ (identity on the underlying spaces, the isomorphism $\mathcal O_X/K\cong i_*\mathcal O_Z$ on structure sheaves) is an isomorphism of closed subschemes of $X$ over $X$. [F4, F5, step 1.2]

$Z_{\mathcal I}$ is a closed subscheme with kernel $\mathcal I$: the inclusion $i:Z_{\mathcal I}\to X$ is a homeomorphism onto the closed subset $V(\mathcal I)$ by construction. On each affine chart $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$, step 1.1 gives $\mathcal I|_U=\widetilde J$ and step 2.1 identifies $Z_{\mathcal I}\cap U$ with $\operatorname{Spec}(A/J)$. On every distinguished open $D(f)\subseteq U$, both $(\mathcal O_U/\widetilde J)(D(f))$ and $(i_*\mathcal O_{Z_{\mathcal I}})(D(f))$ are $(A/J)_f$ by [F2], [F4] and step 2.1. Since distinguished opens form a basis, the natural map $\mathcal O_X/\mathcal I\to i_*\mathcal O_{Z_{\mathcal I}}$ is an isomorphism of sheaves. Thus $\mathcal O_X\to i_*\mathcal O_{Z_{\mathcal I}}$ is surjective and $i$ is a closed immersion by [F4], with kernel $\mathcal I$. In the extreme case $\mathcal I=\mathcal O_X$ the quotient is the zero sheaf, whose support is $\varnothing$, giving the empty subscheme; for $\mathcal I=0$ the immersion is the identity of $X$. This constructs $\mathcal I\mapsto Z_{\mathcal I}$ with the asserted properties. [F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1]

The two constructions are inverse bijections: starting from a quasi-coherent ideal sheaf $\mathcal I$, step 3.1 gives $K_{Z_{\mathcal I}}=\ker(\mathcal O_X\to\mathcal O_X/\mathcal I)=\mathcal I$, including $\mathcal I=\mathcal O_X$; starting from a closed immersion $i:Z\to X$, step 1.2 gives a quasi-coherent ideal sheaf $K_Z$ and step 2.2 gives $Z_{K_Z}\cong Z$ over $X$. Hence $\mathcal I\mapsto Z_{\mathcal I}$ and $Z\mapsto K_Z$ are mutually inverse bijections between quasi-coherent ideal sheaves and closed subschemes, and the empty subscheme is covered by the case $\mathcal I=\mathcal O_X$ on the one side and by the empty closed immersion, whose kernel is $\mathcal O_X$, on the other. [F6, step 3.1, step 1.2, step 2.2]

boundaries.evidence: The statement compares finite type with coherence over arbitrary bases; the empty scheme and the zero module are unproblematic, since the zero sheaf is coherent and of finite type by the definition, and the example witnessing the failure is the structure sheaf of a nonempty, nonzero spectrum.

The zero module satisfies both sides of the distinction, being coherent and of finite type by the statement of the definition; the warning in this remark concerns nonzero, indeed locally free, examples such as the module $A$ of the definition's example, so it does not rest on any behaviour of zero objects.

The example in the definition is the free module of rank one $A$ over the non-Noetherian ring $A$, that is the case of a single generator; it is finitely presented yet admits an endomorphism with non-finitely-generated kernel, which is exactly the unit-rank case in which the coherence test fails.

The degenerate instances are the point of the remark: the base ring $A$ of the example is non-Noetherian and non-reduced, its ideal of relations is not finitely generated, and the module in question is free of finite rank; the statement of the remark is that in this degeneracy the implication from finite presentation (or finite local freeness) to coherence fails.

The endpoints of the coherence test are the finite ranks $n=0$ and $n=1$ of the test morphism; the trivial test with $n=0$ has zero kernel and is unproblematic, while the example uses the extreme nonzero case $n=1$ of an endomorphism of the structure sheaf, where the kernel condition already fails.

The remark introduces no selection at all: the ring, the module $A$ and the endomorphism of the example are explicit, and the cited theorem and definition are invoked only for their statements. The Axiom of Choice enters only as inherited by the coherence theory through the theorem cited in the statement, with no new choice principle used.

The direction that survives is the statement of the theorem: on a locally Noetherian scheme finite type implies coherence, hence coherent and finite type coincide there; the remark explicitly restricts that implication to locally Noetherian bases and warns that its hypothesis is used essentially.

The direction that fails is the reverse one: without the locally Noetherian hypothesis, finite type (even finite presentation and finite local freeness) does not imply coherence. The counterexample is the rank-one free module $A$ of the definition's example on the non-Noetherian spectrum $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$, whose structure sheaf carries a morphism with non-finitely-generated kernel, so it is not coherent there.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $S=\bigoplus_{d\ge0}S_d$ be a commutative nonnegatively graded ring
([[def-graded-ring-and-graded-module]]) and let
$$S_+=\bigoplus_{d>0}S_d$$
be its **irrelevant ideal**. Indeed $S_+$ is an ideal: it is an additive
subgroup, and for $s_i\in S_i$ with $i>0$ and $s_j\in S_j$ with $j\ge0$ one has
$s_is_j\in S_{i+j}$ with $i+j>0$.

An ideal $\mathfrak p\subseteq S$ is **homogeneous** when it is generated by
homogeneous elements. Equivalently, $\mathfrak p$ is homogeneous when for every
$a\in\mathfrak p$ each homogeneous component of $a$ lies in $\mathfrak p$: if
$\mathfrak p=(h_\lambda)$ with $h_\lambda$ homogeneous and
$a=\sum_d a_d\in\mathfrak p$, then each $a_d$ is an $S$-linear combination of
the generators and so lies in $\mathfrak p$. A homogeneous ideal is a
**homogeneous prime** when it is prime as an ideal.

The **projective spectrum** $\operatorname{Proj}S$ is the set of homogeneous
prime ideals $\mathfrak p\subseteq S$ with
$$S_+\not\subseteq\mathfrak p .$$
For a homogeneous ideal $I\subseteq S$ put
$$V_+(I)=\{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Proj}S:I\subseteq\mathfrak p\},$$
and declare these the **closed sets** of the Zariski topology on
$\operatorname{Proj}S$; a subset is **open** when its complement is closed. The
family $\{V_+(I)\}$ is closed under the topological operations (see the
Remarks), so the declaration defines a topology, which is the trace on
$\operatorname{Proj}S$ of the Zariski topology of $\operatorname{Spec}S$
([[def-affine-scheme-spectrum]]) restricted to the homogeneous primes that do
not contain $S_+$, presented by homogeneous generators.

The **zero ring is allowed**: for $S=0$ the ring has no prime ideals at all, so
$\operatorname{Proj}0=\varnothing$ with its unique topology and
$V_+(I)=\varnothing$ for every homogeneous ideal $I\subseteq 0$. Consequently
$\operatorname{Proj}S$ may be empty for nonzero $S$ as well, and all statements
below are meant to include the empty case.

Let $S=\bigoplus_{d\ge0}S_d$ be a commutative nonnegatively graded ring with
projective spectrum $\operatorname{Proj}S$ as in
[[def-proj-graded-ring-points]]. For a homogeneous element $f\in S_+$ of
positive degree set
$$D_+(f)=\{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Proj}S: f\notin\mathfrak p\}.$$
These are the **standard opens** of $\operatorname{Proj}S$.

Prime ideals and maximal ideals in a commutative ring.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. A proper ideal $P\subsetneq R$ is **prime** when
$ab\in P$ implies $a\in P$ or $b\in P$. A proper ideal $M\subsetneq R$ is
**maximal** when there is no proper ideal strictly between $M$ and $R$; equivalently,
it is a maximal element of the poset of proper ideals ordered by inclusion.

For a commutative ring $R$ and $f\in R$, the powers
$$ S_f=\{1,f,f^2,\ldots\}=\{f^n:n\in\mathbb N\} $$
form a multiplicative subset. The **principal localisation** of $R$ at $f$ is
$$ R_f=S_f^{-1}R. $$
Its elements may be written $r/f^n$. In particular, $R_1$ is canonically isomorphic to $R$, while $R_0$ is the zero ring.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $S\subseteq R$ multiplicative. For $r,r'\in R$ and $s,s'\in S$,
$$ \frac r s=\frac{r'}{s'}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u(rs'-r's)=0\text{ for some }u\in S, $$
and
$$ \frac r s=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad ur=0\text{ for some }u\in S. $$
Consequently
$$ \ker\lambda_S=\{r\in R:ur=0\text{ for some }u\in S\}. $$
The map $\lambda_S$ is injective if and only if every $u\in S$ has trivial annihilator. If $R$ is nonzero, this is equivalent to $0\notin S$ and no member of $S$ being a zero divisor.
Moreover, $S^{-1}R$ is the zero ring if and only if $0\in S$.

A **nonnegatively graded ring** is a commutative ring
$$ S=\bigoplus_{n\ge 0} S_n $$
such that $S_nS_m\subseteq S_{n+m}$ for all $m,n\ge 0$. An element of $S_n$ is
called **homogeneous of degree $n$**.

If $S$ is graded, a **graded $S$-module** is an $S$-module
$$ M=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb Z} M_n $$
with $S_iM_j\subseteq M_{i+j}$ for all $i\ge 0$ and $j\in\mathbb Z$. An element
of $M_j$ is homogeneous of degree $j$.

For an integer $a$, the **twist** $M(a)$ is the graded module with
$$ M(a)_n=M_{n+a}. $$
Thus a homogeneous element of degree $n+a$ in $M$ is viewed as degree $n$ in
$M(a)$.

The graded ring is **standard graded over $S_0$** when $S$ is generated as an
$S_0$-algebra by finitely many degree-one elements.

For a homogeneous $a$ of degree $kd$ the element $a^d/f^{\deg a}=a^d/f^{kd}=(a/f^k)^d$ lies in $S_{(f)}$, since $a^d$ is homogeneous of degree $kd^2=kd\cdot d$ with $k d^2=(kd)\cdot d$; this power test is the basis of both constructions.

For a prime $\mathfrak q\subseteq S_{(f)}$, the set $P(\mathfrak q)$ is closed under addition inside each degree: if $a,b\in P(\mathfrak q)\cap S_e$, then expanding the $2d$-th power and grouping the terms of $(a+b)^{2d}/f^{2e}$ by the number $i$ of $a$-factors, every monomial $a^ib^{2d-i}/f^{2e}$ has $i\ge d$ or $2d-i\ge d$, and correspondingly equals $(a^d/f^e)\cdot(a^{i-d}b^{2d-i}/f^e)$ or $(b^d/f^e)\cdot(a^ib^{d-i}/f^e)$, a product of an element of $\mathfrak q$ (namely $a^d/f^e$ or $b^d/f^e$, which lies in $\mathfrak q$ because $a,b\in P(\mathfrak q)$ and $e=\deg a=\deg b$) with an element of $S_{(f)}$ as in step 1.1; hence $((a+b)^d/f^e)^2=(a+b)^{2d}/f^{2e}\in\mathfrak q$, and since $\mathfrak q$ is prime and radical, $(a+b)^d/f^e\in\mathfrak q$, that is, $a+b\in P(\mathfrak q)\cap S_e$.

For a homogeneous prime $\mathfrak p\subseteq S$ with $f\notin\mathfrak p$, membership in $Q(\mathfrak p)$ is independent of a fraction representation: if $a/f^k=b/f^m$ in $S_f$, [F5] gives $f^N(f^ma-f^kb)=0$ for some $N$, and primality with $f\notin\mathfrak p$ gives $a\in\mathfrak p$ if and only if $b\in\mathfrak p$. The set $Q(\mathfrak p)$ of the Statement is therefore an ideal of $S_{(f)}$: it contains $0=0/f^0$; if $a/f^k,b/f^m\in Q(\mathfrak p)$ then their sum has numerator $af^m+bf^k\in\mathfrak p$, homogeneous of degree $(k+m)d$, and multiplication by any fraction $c/f^\ell\in S_{(f)}$ gives numerator $ac\in\mathfrak p$. It is proper because $1=f^k/f^k\in Q(\mathfrak p)$ would force $f\in\mathfrak p$. It is prime because if a product represented by $ab/f^{k+m}$ lies in $Q(\mathfrak p)$, then $ab\in\mathfrak p$, so the homogeneous numerator $a$ or $b$ lies in $\mathfrak p$ and the corresponding factor lies in $Q(\mathfrak p)$. [F3, F5, step 1.1]

For a prime $\mathfrak q\subseteq S_{(f)}$, the span $\mathfrak p(\mathfrak q)=\bigoplus_e\bigl(P(\mathfrak q)\cap S_e\bigr)$ is a homogeneous ideal of $S$: it contains $0$ and is closed under addition componentwise by step 2.1. For homogeneous $s\in S_m$ and $a\in P(\mathfrak q)\cap S_e$ one has $(sa)^d/f^{e+m}=(a^d/f^e)\cdot(s^d/f^m)\in\mathfrak q$ because $s^d/f^m\in S_{(f)}$, so $sa\in P(\mathfrak q)$. Distributing products of finite sums of homogeneous elements extends this closure to arbitrary $s\in S$ and arbitrary elements of the direct sum. Thus the direct sum is an ideal, and it is exactly the ideal generated by the homogeneous set $P(\mathfrak q)$. [F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

otin\mathfrak p(\mathfrak q)$: if $a,b\in S$ are homogeneous with $ab\in\mathfrak p(\mathfrak q)$, then $(ab)^d/f^{\deg a+\deg b}=(a^d/f^{\deg a})(b^d/f^{\deg b})\in\mathfrak q$, so one of the two factors lies in $\mathfrak q$, that is, $a\in P(\mathfrak q)$ or $b\in P(\mathfrak q)$. Thus $uv

The composite $Q\circ\mathfrak p(\cdot)$ is the identity: for a prime $\mathfrak q\subseteq S_{(f)}$ and an element $y=a/f^k\in S_{(f)}$ with $\deg a=kd$, one has $y\in Q(\mathfrak p(\mathfrak q))$ if and only if $a\in\mathfrak p(\mathfrak q)$, if and only if $y^d=a^d/f^{kd}\in\mathfrak q$, if and only if $y\in\mathfrak q$, the last step because $\mathfrak q$ is prime and hence radical in both directions.
